notes: Source: a short English retelling of the fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm (Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 1812). The tale is in the public domain; this retelling was written for this project and is released under CC0 (public domain dedication).

sentences.text: Once upon a time a poor woodcutter lived at the edge of a great forest with his two children and their stepmother.
The boy was called Hansel and his little sister was called Gretel.
The woodcutter was their father.
He loved his children, but the family had almost nothing to eat.
The stepmother was cruel and she hated the children.
One evening the stepmother spoke to the father.
"There is not enough bread for four," she said.
"Tomorrow you must take the children deep into the forest and leave them there."
The father wept, but he agreed in the end.
Hansel heard every word through the thin wall of the bedroom.
He told his sister about the plan.
"Do not cry, Gretel," he whispered.
"I will find a way."
Hansel crept out of the house at night and filled his pockets with white pebbles.
In the morning the father led the children into the forest.
Hansel dropped a pebble on the path every few steps.
The father lit a fire and went away.
The children waited until the moon rose.
The white pebbles shone in the moonlight and showed them the way home.
The father was glad to see them, but the stepmother was furious.
A few days later the stepmother made the father take the children into the forest again.
This time Hansel had no pebbles, so he scattered crumbs of bread on the path.
The birds ate every crumb.
When night came, Hansel and Gretel were lost.
They walked for three days and grew hungry and tired.
At last they saw a white bird.
It led them to a little house in a clearing.
The walls of the house were made of bread and the roof was made of cake.
The windows were made of clear sugar.
Hansel ate a piece of the roof and Gretel ate a piece of the window.
"Nibble, nibble, little mouse, who is nibbling at my house?" called a voice from inside.
The door opened and an old woman came out.
She was a witch, but she smiled kindly at the children.
"Come in, dear children," said the witch.
"You will have food and a warm bed."
Hansel and Gretel followed her into the house.
They did not know that the witch built her house of bread to catch hungry children.
Early the next morning the witch locked Hansel in a small cage.
She made Gretel carry water and cook for her brother.
"Fatten him up," said the witch.
"I will eat him when he is fat."
Every day the witch came to the cage and said, "Hansel, put out your finger so that I can feel how fat you are."
Hansel held out a thin bone instead of his finger.
The witch could not see well, so she thought the bone was his finger.
She was angry that Hansel stayed so thin.
After four weeks the witch lost her patience.
"Gretel, climb into the oven and see if it is hot enough," she ordered.
Gretel guessed the witch's plan.
"I do not know how," said Gretel.
"Show me first."
The witch bent over and put her head into the oven.
Gretel pushed her with all her strength and shut the iron door.
The witch burned in her own oven.
Gretel ran to the cage and set her brother free.
"The witch is dead!" she cried.
Hansel and Gretel hugged each other and danced with joy.
They found pearls and jewels in every corner of the witch's house.
They filled their pockets and their aprons and set off for home.
On their way they came to a wide lake.
A white duck carried Hansel and Gretel across the water, one after the other.
Soon they saw the woodcutter's house through the trees.
They ran inside and threw their arms around their father.
The father had not had a happy hour since he lost the children.
The stepmother was dead.
Gretel shook out her apron and the pearls rolled over the floor.
From that day on the family lived together without worry, and the father was never poor again.
